# The angular system and the exact free tail {#sec-angular-system}

## The physical question {#sec-angular-system-question}

@sec-fourier-adjoint reduced the transport problem, at one wavelength and one
$(\mathbf k,\omega)$, to a single equation on the sphere of directions:
$$
(D-V)h=1,\qquad
D=d_0+ik\mu,\quad d_0=\mu_t-\frac{i\omega}{v},\quad
\mu=\hat{\mathbf k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf s}.
$$ {#eq-angular-starting-point}
The right-hand side is the isotropic detector functional of
@sec-optical-module; the source has already left the problem by reciprocity.
@eq-angular-starting-point is exact and completely useless for computation
until $h$ is given finitely many numbers.

Expanding in spherical harmonics does that, and it does something better than
merely discretising: the two operators become as simple as they can be. The
scattering operator turns diagonal, because the phase function depends only on
the angle between directions. The streaming multiplier $\mu$ turns
tridiagonal, because $\mu P_\ell$ is a combination of $P_{\ell-1}$ and
$P_{\ell+1}$ and nothing else. What is left is a tridiagonal linear system,
which is the cheapest dense-looking object in numerical linear algebra.

One thing spoils the picture, and this chapter is mostly about it. The system
is **infinite**. Truncating the scattering operator at degree $L$ is a
modelling decision with a controllable error; truncating the *system* at degree
$L$ by declaring $h_{L+1}=0$ is not, because it imposes a boundary condition in
angular degree that the transfer equation never asked for. The two are
routinely confused. The resolution is that above $L$ the system is free — no
scattering, no right-hand side — and a free tail can be eliminated **exactly**,
in closed form, by one number added to one matrix entry. Getting that number
reliably is the rest of the chapter, and it turns out to be a question about
which of two branches of a recurrence the physical solution follows.

## Assumptions and definitions {#sec-angular-system-assumptions}

One wavelength, one fixed pair $(k,\omega)$, a reciprocal Henyey--Greenstein
medium, and the isotropic detector functional $a=1$. The medium is homogeneous
and unbounded, so @eq-angular-starting-point holds independently at each
$(\mathbf k,\omega)$, and $\mu_a>0$ so that @eq-coercivity applies.

### Why only $m=0$ {#sec-angular-system-m-zero}

Put the polar axis of the spherical-harmonic expansion along
$\hat{\mathbf k}$. Then three things are invariant under rotations about that
axis: $D$, because it depends on the direction only through
$\mu=\hat{\mathbf k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf s}$; the scattering operator $V$, because
its kernel depends only on $\hat{\mathbf s}\cdot\hat{\mathbf s}'$; and the
right-hand side, which is the constant $1$. A rotationally invariant equation
with a rotationally invariant right-hand side has a rotationally invariant
solution, so
$$
h=h(\mu),
$$
and in spherical-harmonic language only the $m=0$ coefficients are populated.

Two clarifications, because this is where the reasoning is easy to break.
The emission direction of the source does **not** spoil the symmetry, for the
simple reason that the source is not in @eq-angular-starting-point at all:
reciprocity moved it to a contraction performed afterwards
(@eq-adjoint-response). A *directional detector* does spoil it, because then
the right-hand side is a function of the angle to the module axis rather than a
constant, and the axis need not be along $\hat{\mathbf k}$; the problem then
splits into fixed-$m$ blocks. That case is @sec-directional-om and no $m\ne0$
appears in this chapter.

### The orthonormal basis {#sec-angular-system-basis}

Use the Legendre polynomials normalised on $[-1,1]$,
$$
p_\ell(\mu)=\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{2}}\,P_\ell(\mu),
\qquad
\int_{-1}^{1}p_\ell(\mu)\,p_j(\mu)\,\mathrm d\mu=\delta_{\ell j},
$$ {#eq-orthonormal-basis}
and expand
$$
h(\mu)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}h_\ell\,p_\ell(\mu).
$$ {#eq-h-expansion}
Three similar-looking symbols are used in this book and they are not the same
thing: $P_\ell$ is the ordinary Legendre polynomial, $p_\ell$ is the
orthonormal basis function of @eq-orthonormal-basis, and $p_g$ is the phase
function @eq-hg. Only $p_\ell$ appears below.

The right-hand side of @eq-angular-starting-point is the constant $1$, whose
coefficients follow from $\int_{-1}^{1}P_\ell\,\mathrm d\mu=2\delta_{\ell0}$:
$$
\int_{-1}^{1}p_\ell(\mu)\,\mathrm d\mu=\sqrt2\,\delta_{\ell0} .
$$ {#eq-constant-projection}
The entire forcing of the problem sits in one entry.

## Derivation {#sec-angular-system-derivation}

**The scattering operator is diagonal.** @eq-hg-eigenvalues already gives the
Legendre eigenvalues of the Henyey--Greenstein kernel, so for an axially
symmetric $f$,
$$
V\,p_\ell=\gamma_\ell\,p_\ell,\qquad
\gamma_\ell=\begin{cases}\mu_s\,g^{\ell}, & \ell\le L,\\[2pt] 0, & \ell>L.\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-gamma}
Setting $\gamma_\ell=0$ above $L$ is the **only** approximation made to the
physics in this chapter. It replaces the infinite-rank Henyey--Greenstein
operator by a finite-rank one, and it is an angular truncation of the
*medium*, not a truncation of the number of collisions and not a truncation of
free streaming, both of which remain exact to all degrees.

The $\ell=0$ diagonal deserves its own line. Since $\gamma_0=\mu_s$,
$$
d_0-\gamma_0=\mu_t-\frac{i\omega}{v}-\mu_s=\mu_a-\frac{i\omega}{v},
$$ {#eq-row-zero}
and the extinction has cancelled down to the absorption. This is exactly the
angular form of the photon-number balance @eq-spectral-number-balance: the
$\ell=0$ moment is the photon number, scattering does not change it, and what
remains is absorption plus a time derivative. An implementation whose first
diagonal entry still contains $\mu_s$ has lost that cancellation somewhere.

**The streaming operator is tridiagonal.** From the standard recurrence
$(\ell+1)P_{\ell+1}=(2\ell+1)\mu P_\ell-\ell P_{\ell-1}$, converting to the
normalised basis gives
$$
\mu\,p_\ell=a_\ell\,p_{\ell-1}+a_{\ell+1}\,p_{\ell+1},
\qquad
a_\ell=\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{4\ell^2-1}},\quad a_0=0 .
$$ {#eq-streaming-recurrence}
Multiplication by $\mu$ therefore couples each degree to its two neighbours and
to nothing else.

**The system.** Project @eq-angular-starting-point onto $p_\ell$, using
@eq-gamma, @eq-streaming-recurrence and @eq-constant-projection:
$$
ik\,a_\ell\,h_{\ell-1}
+(d_0-\gamma_\ell)\,h_\ell
+ik\,a_{\ell+1}\,h_{\ell+1}
=\sqrt2\,\delta_{\ell0},
\qquad \ell=0,1,2,\dots
$$ {#eq-angular-system}
Written out, the first three rows are
$$
\begin{aligned}
(d_0-\mu_s)\,h_0&+ik\,a_1h_1&&=\sqrt2,\\
ik\,a_1h_0+{}&(d_0-\mu_sg)\,h_1+ik\,a_2h_2&&=0,\\
ik\,a_2h_1+{}&(d_0-\mu_sg^2)\,h_2+ik\,a_3h_3&&=0,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-first-rows}
with $a_1=1/\sqrt3$, $a_2=2/\sqrt{15}$, $a_3=3/\sqrt{35}$. Every entry has a
single origin: the diagonal is $d_0$ from the multiplier minus the scattering
eigenvalue of that degree, and the off-diagonals are $ik$ times the coupling
coefficient of @eq-streaming-recurrence. The matrix is **complex symmetric**,
$M_{\ell,\ell+1}=M_{\ell+1,\ell}$, which is @eq-complex-symmetric in this
basis. It is **not** Hermitian as soon as $k\ne0$ or $\omega\ne0$, because the
off-diagonals are then imaginary and the diagonal is complex.

### Why hard truncation is wrong {#sec-angular-system-hard-truncation}

Keep $\ell=0,\dots,L$ and look at what row $L$ needs:
$$
ik\,a_L\,h_{L-1}+(d_0-\gamma_L)\,h_L+ik\,a_{L+1}\,h_{L+1}=0 .
$$
It contains $h_{L+1}$, which is outside the retained block. Setting
$h_{L+1}=0$ closes the system, and that is precisely the problem: it is an
extra condition, imposed in angular degree, that nothing in the transfer
equation implies. The transfer equation says $\gamma_{L+1}=0$ — the medium
does not scatter into that degree — but streaming still populates it, and
$h_{L+1}$ is not small merely because $\gamma_{L+1}$ is zero.

The consequence is a solution of the wrong problem, and the error does not go
away quietly: it is worst exactly where $L$ is small and the calculation is
cheap. @sec-angular-system-example measures it. Hard truncation appears in
this book only as a named rejected reference, never as an option.

### The exact free tail {#sec-angular-system-tail}

Above $L$ the system is free: $\gamma_\ell=0$ and the right-hand side vanishes,
so every row $\ell>L$ reads
$$
ik\,a_\ell\,h_{\ell-1}+d_0\,h_\ell+ik\,a_{\ell+1}\,h_{\ell+1}=0 .
$$ {#eq-free-rows}
A second-order recurrence has a two-dimensional solution space, and the two
branches behave oppositely: one decays with degree, the other grows. Which one
the physical solution follows is decided, not chosen. $h$ is a function on
$[-1,1]$ that is square integrable, so by @eq-h-expansion its coefficients are
square summable and in particular $h_\ell\to0$. The growing branch is therefore
excluded, and above $L$ the solution is proportional to the **minimal**,
decaying branch.

Introduce the free moments, the coefficients of the unscattered multiplier
alone,
$$
b_\ell(k,\omega)=\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{p_\ell(\mu)}{d_0+ik\mu}\,\mathrm d\mu ,
$$ {#eq-free-moments}
which satisfy the same homogeneous recurrence @eq-free-rows and are themselves
the coefficients of a square-integrable function, hence the minimal branch.
Because a ratio of consecutive terms is independent of how a branch is
normalised, the solution and the free moments share it:
$$
r_\ell=\frac{b_{\ell+1}}{b_\ell}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
h_{L+1}=r_L\,h_L .
$$ {#eq-tail-ratio}
Substituting into row $L$ eliminates $h_{L+1}$ and closes the system at size
$L+1$ with a single modified entry:
$$
M_{LL}=d_0-\gamma_L+ik\,a_{L+1}\,r_L,
$$ {#eq-tail-correction}
while every other entry is untouched,
$$
M_{\ell\ell}=d_0-\gamma_\ell,\qquad
M_{\ell,\ell-1}=ik\,a_\ell,\qquad
M_{\ell,\ell+1}=ik\,a_{\ell+1}.
$$ {#eq-matrix-entries}

@eq-tail-correction is the **exact Schur complement of the free tail**. In
block form the infinite matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\ C&E\end{pmatrix}$ with
$E$ the free block above $L$; the reduced operator is $A-BE^{-1}C$, and since
$B$ and $C$ each have a single non-zero entry $ik\,a_{L+1}$, that correction is
rank one and lands on the last diagonal. No series is truncated and no
remainder is dropped.

Two qualifications keep the word *exact* honest. It is exact **relative to the
finite-rank scattering model** @eq-gamma: the tail is free because
$\gamma_{\ell>L}=0$ was assumed, and it is that assumption, not the elimination,
that approximates the medium. And it is exact only above the support of both
the scattering operator and the right-hand side — which here is degree $L$,
since @eq-constant-projection puts the forcing at $\ell=0$ alone.

### The free moments and the minimal solution {#sec-angular-system-moments}

Work with the unnormalised moments $F_\ell=\int P_\ell/(d_0+ik\mu)\,\mathrm
d\mu$, so that $b_\ell=\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/2}\,F_\ell$, and set
$$
z=\frac{i\,d_0}{k}.
$$ {#eq-z}
The first two are elementary:
$$
F_0=\frac{2}{k}\arctan\frac{k}{d_0},
\qquad
F_1=z\,F_0+\frac{2}{ik},
$$ {#eq-f0-f1}
and the rest satisfy the Legendre recurrence in $z$,
$$
F_{\ell+1}=\frac{(2\ell+1)\,z\,F_\ell-\ell\,F_{\ell-1}}{\ell+1}.
$$ {#eq-forward-recurrence}

Naming the two branches makes the instability concrete rather than
metaphorical. Since $d_0+ik\mu=ik(\mu-z)$, the moments are
$F_\ell=-2Q_\ell(z)/(ik)$, where $Q_\ell$ is the Legendre function of the
second kind. @eq-forward-recurrence is satisfied by both $P_\ell(z)$ and
$Q_\ell(z)$; off the cut, $Q_\ell(z)$ decays with degree and $P_\ell(z)$ grows.
The physical moments are the $Q$ branch. Round-off in a forward sweep injects a
small amount of the $P$ branch at every step, and that contamination grows
while the wanted solution shrinks, so the computed $F_\ell$ eventually consists
almost entirely of the branch that should not be there. This is not a statement
that "the physical solution decays" — it is a statement about which of two
named, explicit solutions of the same recurrence the arithmetic drifts towards.

### Miller's backward ratios {#sec-angular-system-miller}

Run the recurrence in the direction in which the wanted branch *grows* and the
unwanted one shrinks. For
$$
R_\ell=\frac{F_{\ell+1}}{F_\ell}
$$
dividing @eq-forward-recurrence by $F_\ell$ and rearranging gives
$$
R_{\ell-1}=\frac{\ell}{(2\ell+1)\,z-(\ell+1)\,R_\ell},
$$ {#eq-backward-ratio}
a backward recurrence, and the ratio in the normalised basis is
$$
r_\ell=\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+3}{2\ell+1}}\;R_\ell .
$$ {#eq-normalised-ratio}
Started from an inaccurate value at a sufficiently deep degree,
@eq-backward-ratio forgets the seed: each step damps the contribution of the
dominant branch, so the error decays as the sweep descends. The depth needed is
set by how fast the minimal branch decays. Writing $\rho$ for the asymptotic
per-degree ratio of the minimal branch, the decay rate is
$$
\eta=-\ln\lvert\rho\rvert,
$$ {#eq-decay-rate}
and the implementation chooses per wavenumber:

- **forward** when $\eta\,(N+3)<3$ — the decay over the degrees of interest is
  too weak for contamination to matter, and @eq-forward-recurrence is used
  directly, the ratio being formed by dividing two moments that are both of
  ordinary size;
- **Miller** otherwise, seeded at depth $N+1+\max\!\bigl(32,\lceil
  28/\eta\rceil\bigr)$ and swept down with @eq-backward-ratio. Here the ratios
  are produced *before* any moment is formed, precisely because at these
  depths the moments themselves underflow; the moments are then rebuilt from
  $F_0$ by taking a running product of the ratios.

The constants $3$, $32$ and $28$ are implementation safety choices validated
for the present double-precision code. They are not physical parameters, they
are not claimed optimal, and a change of precision or of the degree range would
require revalidating them rather than reusing them.

### The special case $k=0$ {#sec-angular-system-zero-k}

At $k=0$ the multiplier loses its direction dependence, $D=d_0$, and
@eq-free-moments becomes $\int p_\ell/d_0$, so by
@eq-constant-projection
$$
b_0=\frac{\sqrt2}{d_0},\qquad b_{\ell>0}=0 .
$$ {#eq-zero-k}
Once two consecutive moments are both zero their literal quotient is $0/0$,
not a defined ratio. The implementation never forms that quotient: on the
$k=0$ branch it stores every continuation ratio as zero, the value that safely
propagates the exact zero coefficients and makes the tail correction vanish.
The off-diagonals vanish, and the matrix is diagonal with entries
$d_0-\gamma_\ell$; the solution is
$h_0=\sqrt2/(d_0-\mu_s)$ and nothing else. This is a separate branch in the
code, not a limit reached by dividing by a small $k$: @eq-z and
@eq-f0-f1 both divide by $k$, and evaluating them at $k=10^{-15}$ instead of
taking the branch would be arithmetic on the edge of the representable range
for no reason.

### Output degree and scattering degree {#sec-angular-system-degrees}

Two degrees appear and they are not interchangeable. $L$ is the **scattering
degree**: it truncates @eq-gamma and fixes the size $L+1$ of the solve. $J$ is
the **output degree**: how many angular coefficients the later inversion in
space will ask for. Increasing $J$ must not increase the solve, and it does
not — above $L$ the coefficients are continued by the same exact free ratios of
@eq-tail-ratio, which are already available. @sec-scattering-orders is where
$J$ acquires its meaning; here it is only a length.

Neither $L$ nor $J$ is a number of collisions. Nothing in this chapter counts
collisions at all.

### Invertibility after the elimination {#sec-angular-system-coercivity}

@eq-coercivity applies to the infinite problem with the finite-rank scattering
operator, since the eigenvalues @eq-gamma satisfy
$\lvert\gamma_\ell\rvert\le\mu_s$ exactly as the untruncated ones do, and the
bound used only that. The finite matrix of @eq-matrix-entries and
@eq-tail-correction is the Schur complement of that same invertible operator
with respect to an invertible free block, and a Schur complement of an
invertible operator taken over an invertible block is invertible. The tail term
is therefore part of the exact reduction, not an empirical stabilisation added
to make a solve behave.

One transitional remark closes the chapter. The system @eq-angular-system as
solved here gives the total angular response; splitting it by the number of
scattering events, which the implementation does for reasons of numerical
conditioning, is @sec-scattering-orders, and replacing the constant right-hand
side by a directional module's acceptance, which populates $m\ne0$, is
@sec-directional-om.

## The discrete algorithm {#sec-angular-system-algorithm}

1. **Validate** $L$, $J$, the wavenumbers $k\ge0$, and $d_0$ with
   $\operatorname{Re}d_0>0$.
2. **Compute** the free moments and the successive ratios up to
   $N=\max(L,J)$.
3. **Choose the branch** per wavenumber: forward when $\eta(N+3)<3$, Miller
   otherwise, at that node's own depth.
4. **Take** the terminal ratio $r_L$.
5. **Build** the diagonal $d_0-\gamma_\ell$ from @eq-gamma.
6. **Build** the off-diagonals $ik\,a_\ell$ from @eq-streaming-recurrence.
7. **Add** the tail correction @eq-tail-correction to the last diagonal entry.
8. **Solve** the tridiagonal system, one per wavenumber.
9. **Continue** the coefficients above $L$ up to $J$ with the exact free
   ratios.
10. **Check** that every value is finite, and fail loudly rather than
    returning a silent `nan`.

Step 3 is per wavenumber and not per batch: a single batch-wide depth would
charge every node the margin demanded by the slowest-decaying one.

## Correspondence with the code {#sec-angular-system-code}

| Mathematics | Symbol |
|:--|:--|
| Degree validation | `lighthit.angular._degree` |
| Free moments and ratios, @eq-free-moments and @eq-normalised-ratio | `lighthit.angular._free_moments_and_ratios_numpy` |
| Backend selection | `lighthit.angular._free_moments_and_ratios` |
| Public free moments and the terminal ratio $r_N$ | `lighthit.angular.free_moments_and_tail` |
| The tridiagonal solve with @eq-tail-correction | `lighthit.angular.solve_tail_system` |
| The assembled angular coefficients | `lighthit.angular.angular_components` |
| Independent dense control | `lighthit.angular.dense_finite_rank_reference` |
| Compiled per-node recurrences | `lighthit._angular_numba.free_moments_and_ratios` |
| $L$ and $J$ | `lighthit.green.SolverSettings` |

Symbols beginning with an underscore are implementation details. They are named
here because this chapter is about how the calculation is done, and the reader
should be able to find it; they are not part of the stable interface and may
change without the book changing.

`angular_components` returns its result in parts. Their separate meaning is
@sec-scattering-orders; everything in this chapter uses only their sum, which
is the solution of @eq-angular-system.

## A worked number {#sec-angular-system-example}

Every object in this chapter is rebuilt from its definition in the example --
the basis, the coupling coefficients, the matrix, the tail correction -- and
then compared against the package. Public synthetic medium only, no spatial
cache, and Numba is used when present but never required.

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \
NUMBA_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  python scripts/run_angular_system_example.py --output .build/angular-system-example
```

The stored output is `docs/angular-system-example/summary.json`, which carries
the configuration, the library versions, the thread settings and the exact
value of every residual quoted below as a bound.

**Configuration.** $\mu_a=0.04\ \mathrm m^{-1}$, $\mu_s=0.05\ \mathrm m^{-1}$,
$g=0.7$, $n_g=1.35$; $k=0.2\ \mathrm m^{-1}$, $\omega=0$, $L=8$. Then
$d_0=\mu_t=0.09\ \mathrm m^{-1}$, real because $\omega=0$.

**The matrix, entry by entry.** The first three diagonal entries come out as
$0.0400$, $0.0550$, $0.0655\ \mathrm m^{-1}$, which are
$\mu_t-\mu_sg^\ell$ for $\ell=0,1,2$; the first is $\mu_a$ exactly, as
@eq-row-zero requires. The first two off-diagonals are $0.11547\,i$ and
$0.10328\,i\ \mathrm m^{-1}$, which are $ik\,a_1$ and $ik\,a_2$ with
$a_1=1/\sqrt3$ and $a_2=2/\sqrt{15}$. The terminal ratio is
$r_8=-0.6470815\,i$, and the corrected last entry is
$$
M_{88}=\underbrace{0.0871176}_{d_0-\mu_sg^8}
+\underbrace{ik\,a_9\,r_8}_{0.0648082}
=0.1519258\ \mathrm m^{-1},
$$
which can be checked on paper from $a_9=9/\sqrt{323}$. The matrix is exactly
symmetric and exactly tridiagonal, and its distance from its own conjugate
transpose is $0.23\ \mathrm m^{-1}$ — it is not Hermitian, and the example
records that as a positive statement rather than an absence.

**Hard truncation against the exact tail.** Both are compared against
`dense_finite_rank_reference`, an independent dense solve that builds the
angular operator by Gauss quadrature and inverts it directly, at the same
scattering degree:

| $L$ | exact tail | hard truncation |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 3 | $<3\times10^{-13}$ | $1.9\times10^{-1}$ |
| 8 | $<3\times10^{-13}$ | $2.7\times10^{-2}$ |
| 16 | $<3\times10^{-13}$ | $8.3\times10^{-4}$ |
| 32 | $<3\times10^{-13}$ | $7.8\times10^{-7}$ |

Read the two columns differently. The first column gives one conservative
bound for all four measured residuals; their environment-specific values are
kept in the stored JSON rather than frozen into the prose. It is flat at the
level of round-off: the elimination introduces no error of its own, so what is
left is arithmetic, and it does not improve with $L$ because there is nothing
to improve. The hard-truncation column is a convergence study of a *different*
problem: it does converge, from $19\%$ at $L=3$ to $8\times10^{-7}$ at $L=32$,
but it buys with degrees what costs nothing at all when the tail is eliminated.
At the deliberately small illustrative value $L=8$, hard truncation is wrong in
the second decimal place. Current production presets use larger degrees, but
that does not make hard truncation the equation being solved: the exact closure
removes this separate error at every $L$.

**Independent controls.** The package's tridiagonal solve agrees with a dense
solve of the same matrix, and the assembled coefficients agree with the dense
reference, both to better than $10^{-12}$. The terminal ratio $r_8$ agrees with
an independent continued fraction started $400$ degrees deeper with a
deliberately different seed, to better than $10^{-12}$; that both routes agree
so sharply is the point of @eq-backward-ratio — the seed is forgotten.

**The branch decision.** Over 61 wavenumbers spanning $10^{-3}$ to
$40\ \mathrm m^{-1}$ at this $d_0$, the decay rate $\eta$ ranges from
$2.2\times10^{-3}$ to $5.2$. The rule of @sec-angular-system-miller sends the
large-$k$ end forward and the small-$k$ end to Miller. In this diagnostic the
output degree is set equal to the scattering degree, so the table varies the
combined recurrence length $N=\max(L,J)=L$:

| $N=L=J$ | forward nodes | Miller nodes | deepest start |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 3 | 31 | 30 | 59 |
| 8 | 28 | 33 | 100 |
| 16 | 25 | 36 | 169 |
| 32 | 21 | 40 | 339 |

Increasing $N$ tightens the forward criterion, so more nodes take the backward
route and the deepest start grows roughly with the required recurrence length.
In production $J$ can exceed $L$, and then it is $J$, not $L$, that sets this
branch decision and depth.

**$k=0$.** The branch returns $b_0=\sqrt2/d_0$ exactly, every higher moment
identically zero, and every ratio identically zero, so the matrix is diagonal.
These are exact zeros and not small numbers.

**Independence of the output degree.** Solving with $J=L$ and with $J=3L$
leaves the first $L+1$ coefficients unchanged to a relative $10^{-12}$; the
longer run returns more coefficients and does not solve a larger system.

## Checks {#sec-angular-system-checks}

Twenty checks are recorded as booleans in the stored summary, and the script
exits with a failure if any is false.

**The basis.** Orthonormality of $p_\ell$ over a 1024-node Gauss rule,
@eq-streaming-recurrence verified both pointwise and by projection, and
@eq-constant-projection verified against $\sqrt2\,\delta_{\ell0}$ — all below
$10^{-12}$.

**The matrix.** Exactly symmetric; exactly tridiagonal, with every entry
outside the three bands identically zero; not Hermitian; and row zero equal to
$\mu_a-i\omega/v$ to round-off.

**The solves.** The package's tridiagonal routine against a dense solve of the
same matrix, and the assembled coefficients against both that direct solve and
the independent dense reference, all below $10^{-12}$ — with the dense
reference held to $10^{-10}$, since it carries its own angular quadrature
error.

**The tail.** The terminal ratio against a deep independent continued fraction;
the exact-tail solution against the dense reference at four degrees; and hard
truncation required to be at least a thousand times worse at $L=3$, which it is
by twelve orders.

**The special cases and the backends.** The $k=0$ branch returning exact zeros;
independence of the output degree; finiteness everywhere; and NumPy against
Numba below $10^{-12}$ when the optional dependency is installed. When it is
absent the run records that and passes, rather than failing on a missing
optional package.

Nothing here validates the transport chain. What is checked is that the
tridiagonal system is the one derived above, that the tail elimination is exact
to arithmetic, and that hard truncation is not.

## Range of validity {#sec-angular-system-validity}

- **The $m=0$ adjoint problem only**, with an isotropic detector functional and
  a rotationally invariant medium. A directional module breaks the symmetry and
  is @sec-directional-om.
- **Finite-rank scattering.** @eq-gamma is the one approximation; its error is
  controlled by $L$ and is measured in @sec-validation.
- **The free tail is exact only above the support** of both the scattering
  operator and the right-hand side. A right-hand side with content above $L$
  would invalidate @eq-tail-correction as written.
- **$\mu_a>0$**, so that @eq-coercivity holds uniformly and the tridiagonal
  system is invertible for every $(k,\omega)$.
- **Real $k$ and $\omega$**, with $\operatorname{Re}d_0>0$, which the
  implementation requires explicitly.
- **Double precision.** The branch rule and its constants
  $3$, $32$, $28$ were validated for this implementation at this precision and
  carry no guarantee outside it.
- **$J$ is not $L$, and neither is a collision count.** The solve is of size
  $L+1$ whatever $J$ is.
- **Scattering orders are deferred** to @sec-scattering-orders; nothing here
  separates them.

## Exercises {#sec-angular-system-exercises}

1. Derive the normalisation constant of @eq-orthonormal-basis from
   $\int_{-1}^1P_\ell^2\,\mathrm d\mu=2/(2\ell+1)$, and then obtain
   @eq-constant-projection.
2. Derive @eq-streaming-recurrence from the standard Legendre recurrence, and
   verify $a_1=1/\sqrt3$, $a_2=2/\sqrt{15}$, $a_3=3/\sqrt{35}$.
3. Write out rows $0$, $1$ and $2$ of @eq-angular-system explicitly and
   identify the origin of every entry. Then evaluate them for the
   configuration of @sec-angular-system-example and compare with the numbers
   quoted there.
4. Show that $\gamma_0=\mu_s$ makes the first diagonal entry $\mu_a-i\omega/v$,
   and relate the result to @eq-spectral-number-balance. What would a residual
   $\mu_s$ in that entry mean physically?
5. Derive @eq-tail-correction as a Schur complement, starting from the block
   form of the infinite matrix, and show that the correction is rank one.
6. Explain, in terms of @eq-free-rows, why $h_{L+1}=0$ is an extra boundary
   condition. Then estimate from the table in @sec-angular-system-example how
   many extra degrees hard truncation needs to match the exact tail at
   $L=8$.
7. Derive @eq-backward-ratio from @eq-forward-recurrence, and show that an
   error in the seed is damped by a factor of order $\lvert\rho\rvert^2$ per
   step down.
8. Identify the two solutions of @eq-forward-recurrence as $P_\ell(z)$ and
   $Q_\ell(z)$, say which the moments follow, and explain why a forward sweep
   drifts towards the other one.
9. Derive @eq-zero-k directly from @eq-free-moments, and say what goes wrong
   numerically if @eq-f0-f1 is evaluated at $k=10^{-15}$ instead.
10. Show from @eq-tail-ratio that continuing the coefficients above $L$ needs
    no further solve, and hence that the cost of the solve is independent of
    $J$.
11. Suppose the right-hand side is $a(\hat{\mathbf s})$ for a module whose axis
    is not along $\hat{\mathbf k}$. Say which step of the derivation fails
    first, and what replaces @eq-angular-system.
12. Propose a test that would decide whether the Miller constants $32$ and
    $28$ are adequate at a given precision. State what quantity it measures and
    what result would count as a failure.
